keyVerseText: And they journeyed from Bethel; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour. a little: Heb. a little piece of ground
rootMeaning: The root of כִּבְרָה (kibrâh) is כְּבָר (kᵉbâr), which fundamentally conveys the idea of something that is 'already' or 'long ago,' emphasizing an extent or duration of time. As the feminine form, כִּבְרָה shifts this temporal sense into a spatial dimension, referring to a measure of length or distance. This root connection enriches the common English gloss of 'a little' by suggesting not merely a small quantity but a defined extent or portion that is recognized or acknowledged, linking time and space in the Hebrew conceptual world.
usageInScripture: The word כִּבְרָה appears only three times in Scripture, consistently conveying the idea of a short or limited distance or measure. It is most often translated as 'a little' or 'a little way,' reflecting its idiomatic use to indicate a small spatial extent, as seen in the phrase כִּבְרַת הָאָרֶץ ('a distance of land'). This consistent usage underscores the word's role in describing a tangible but limited stretch of ground or travel, emphasizing brevity in physical terms rather than abstract measurement.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כִּבְרָה as a term denoting a small but definite distance invites reflection on the nature of God's providential guidance and timing in Scripture. The word's root meaning of 'already' or 'long ago' combined with a spatial measure suggests that even seemingly small steps or brief journeys are significant within God's unfolding plan. This reminds believers that every part of the spiritual journey, no matter how short or challenging, is under God's sovereign oversight. It encourages faithfulness in the 'little things,' trusting that God works through all stages and distances in the life of His people.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 35:16, the phrase 'a little way' (Heb. כִּבְרָה) highlights the brief distance from Bethel to Ephrath, where Rachel experiences hard labor. This use of כִּבְרָה conveys not just a small spatial measure but a poignant moment on the journey, emphasizing the nearness yet difficulty of the destination. The word enriches the narrative by focusing attention on the immediate, tangible reality of Rachel's trial, reminding readers that God meets His people intimately in their closest and most challenging moments.
